author: Autodesk
description: A graph that demonstrates simulating raindrops with two different methods.
documentation:
## Raindrop Simulation

### What it does

This graph generates the effect of raindrops hitting a surface.

### Inputs and outputs

There are two inputs for this graph, an emission plane for generating particles to act as "droplets" and the mesh generated from input settings on the `basic_rain_simulation` compound.  Optionally, wave simulations can be used as input on the *additional_waves* port of the `basic_rain_simulation` compound.

### How it works

- This graph demonstrates two methods of generating ripples in a dynamic wave simulation.  The first method is particle collision with the water plane, as demonstrated in the graph.  The second method is using a highly thresholded animated noise field.  This method is laid out in the "Rain" Section inside the `basic_rain_simulation` compound.  (Purple Backdrop). 

- The output from the particle simulation is piped into the `basic_rain_simulation` compound.  Dynamic waves are simulated based on either particle position on collision, or a rain map based on fractal noise generated internally, or both.

- One can easily make the simulation seamlessly wrap in space. Using the `output mesh bound scale` - set to one then the previous simulation is used. At larger values the size of the plane will get bigger and the simulation seamlessly wrap in space. The key is that periodic is enabled on the solver settings, as well as decay_width and decay_alpha set to zero which gets rid of the damping at the boundary.

- The particle raindrops in this compound are exaggerated to show the effect better.  For a realistic render, smaller particle sizes and rain magnitudes would be advised.  For closeups more friction is advised to damp out the ripples over time.

_notes.text:
This scene shows generation of dynamic_wave ripples from rain using two methods.

1. Emission from particles

2. Emissions using an animated, thresholded noise field.
emit ripples from the killed particles

One can connect other waves like this ***create_spectral_waves*** to the *addition_waves* for a simulation with more than ripples. Also note that one could do things like add a ***fractal_noise*** to the  *velocity_position* port of the ***dynamic_wave_settings*** (inside ***basic_rain_simulation***) at the start frame, to create a developed wave system.

For close up raindrops the capillary_size is important. Capillary waves are caused by surface tension, not gravity, and move much faster than gravity waves. This causes the characteristic rain drop ripple look as the wave packets expand apart. Note also that for realistic wave speeds you might need substeps depending on how detailed the resolution is. Very fast wave speeds relative to pixel size might need substeps.

To have the ripples die out faster use the friction property.

# Particle Simulation
This section simulates raindrops for collision with the water surface
Resolution values are computed from the inputs *size* and *detail_size*, which ensures we have square pixels.

# Emit into map

This method emits from all particles into the wave map (like a 2d file texture that is projected) with xz bounds It uses the xz positions of the particles and computes the corresponding pixel in the map then adds to that pixel.

# Rain 
This compound outputs a scalar field that thresholds an animated high frequency ***fractal_noise_field*** to create a sparse animated noise simulation that simulates drops hitting the water. One can efficiently simulate any density or number of drop collisions with the water this way.

# Dynamic Waves

We could apply the map to height or velocity_potential, but the later is generally better as it will work better with effects shallow bottom and avoid damping wave motion.

# Create Wave Map

Setup a wave_map (2d pixels) initialized to the rain field. Bounds are disabled so the map will fit to the dynamic_wave simulation.
iterate over all particles and add to the map pixels.

Image schema is currently all internal methods. It is basically a vector2 resolution combined with  linear data arrays. One could look inside the dynamic_wave compounds to see how these work and copy paste them, or perhaps wrap in custom compounds.

wave_maps are image schema objects with one geo data named "map". They also have xz bounding info, although in this case the bounds are disabled and thus the size value needs to be the one used for the dynamic_wave simulation.
Get the uv value (0-1)of the particle for the map
Get the index into the 2d pixel map for the uv value. Image properties are maintained in linear arrays.

# Kill Influence

kill particles when they go below the water height
Emit particles from this plane in the sky.
